source: Ellis et al. (2020/2023) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Wake-sleep loop: wake searches for programs, abstraction sleep compresses solved programs into new library functions, dreaming sleep trains a recognition network on replayed and imagined tasks. Library and search policy bootstrap each other.
numbers: Text editing (SyGuS 2017, 108 problems, 128 generated train tasks): 3.7% solved in 10 min (mean 235 s) before learning; 79.6% after (mean 40 s). CVC4 winner 82.4% at 1 h and 8 CPUs; DreamCoder 84.3% at that budget. List processing: 218 tasks split 50/50, about 20 new routines learned. Physics laws: 93% of 60 laws after 8 cycles. Deeper libraries correlate with tasks solved r=0.79.
limits: Domains are small DSL problems with exact I/O specs and cheap verification. Training takes about a day on 20-100 CPUs; the origami basis run took about five days on 64 CPUs.
agent_relevance: Core template for a subgoal memory: keep verified solutions, compress the recurring parts, reuse them. Needs a cheap exact check to stay safe (our G3).

source: Ellis et al. (2020/2023) DreamCoder ablations: no recognition model, no library growth
finding: Removing either the neural recognition model or library learning lowers held-out solve rates in every domain. The two parts are synergistic: the recognition model leads to deeper libraries and higher asymptotes.
numbers: Mean search time of full system 54.1 s (median 15.0 s). In LOGO graphics and tower building no alternative model solved more than 60% of held-out tasks while DreamCoder reached nearly 100%.
limits: Ablation is on the original symbolic and neural stack, not on LLM-driven search. Memorization baselines (store solved programs unchanged) were weaker but not zero.
agent_relevance: Storage alone is not the gain; compression into abstractions plus a learned guide to when to use them is. Our scaffold has no learned guide, so retrieval quality is the weak point.

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning (Stitch), POPL
finding: Stitch is a symbolic compressor using corpus-guided top-down search with branch and bound. It finds libraries as good as or better than DreamCoder compression at far lower cost and can stop early.
numbers: 3-4 orders of magnitude faster and 2 orders less memory than DreamCoder compression. Large graphics corpora (8 domains): test compression 2.55x-11.57x in 0.19-60.16 s, peak memory 11.21-714.55 MB; DreamCoder timed out on these. Compression ratio near DreamCoder or better in logo; mixed in list domain.
limits: Compression of a corpus of lambda-calculus programs, not solving. Measures description length, not task success.
agent_relevance: Abstraction choice can be a plain program (counted compression gain) rather than a model judgement. Fits our rule that code selects.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code, ICLR
finding: LLM writes programs, Stitch compresses, an LLM auto-documents each abstraction with a name and docstring. Beats DreamCoder online on all three domains, with the largest gains on REGEX and LOGO.
numbers: Online mean solve rate, REGEX/CLEVR/LOGO: DreamCoder 43.93/94.50/28.53 (gain of LILO +33.14/+2.26/+20.42). LLM Solver without library beats DreamCoder on REGEX by +32.20, is -5.83 on CLEVR, +3.60 on LOGO. LILO over LLM Solver: +0.94 (REGEX), +8.09 (CLEVR), +16.82 (LOGO).
limits: Codex (code-davinci-002) for search, gpt-3.5-turbo for docs. Needs language annotations of tasks. Most REGEX gain comes from the LLM prior, not the library. Small benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Honest decomposition: on REGEX the library adds under 1 point over the bare LLM; on LOGO (needs structures the LLM lacks) it adds 17. Library value depends on whether the base model already knows the domain.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO auto-documentation ablation
finding: Giving the LLM raw Stitch abstractions (anonymous names such as fn_42) hurt it. Adding LLM-written names and docstrings recovered much of the loss.
numbers: Raw Stitch abstractions vs LLM Solver baseline: -30.60 (REGEX), -2.91 (CLEVR), -11.11 (LOGO). AutoDoc then adds +9.73 (REGEX), +2.27 (CLEVR), +0.00 (LOGO) over the naive condition. LOGO limited by semantic errors in documentation.
quote: naively providing a LLM with Stitch abstractions measurably degraded its ability to solve tasks
limits: Single model family, single run protocol; LOGO shows docs can be wrong and not help.
agent_relevance: A stored helper the model cannot read is worse than no helper. If our agent stores subgoal solutions, each needs a readable name and a one-line purpose, ideally verified against its behaviour.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO offline test of learned libraries and cost analysis
finding: Final LILO libraries help plain enumerative search even without language. One LLM synthesis iteration costs about the same as 48 CPU-hours of DreamCoder search.
numbers: Offline gain over base DSL: DreamCoder +19.6 (REGEX), +62.46 (CLEVR), +29.73 (LOGO); LILO +42.27, +63.43, +43.24. Typical iteration uses 0.8M-1.2M GPT tokens. Cost: CLEVR (short timeout) enumeration is 2-2.5x cheaper than LLM search; LOGO about equal. Offline LILO 64.27/92.56/41.14 vs DreamCoder 41.60/91.59/30.63.
limits: Prices at 2023 gpt-3.5 rates ($0.002 per 1K tokens). Cost parity is market-dependent.
agent_relevance: A library built by an LLM loop is a durable, model-free asset for later search. Tokens per iteration are large, so library building must be budgeted.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO appendix C.2: can an LLM do the compression step?
finding: GPT-4 asked to propose abstractions that compress solved programs failed to match Stitch, even with best-effort prompt engineering and clustered examples.
numbers: Stitch compression ratio 1.5-3.5x over solved tasks; GPT-4 produced no meaningful compression. Authors report the prompt effort was much larger than for the solver and gave only negative results.
limits: GPT-4 (2023) only; newer reasoning models not tested. Authors admit the prompt space is open.
agent_relevance: Supports our rule that the program, not the model, does counting and compression gain. Let code pick which fragment is worth keeping.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring Programs to Discover Generalizable Abstractions, ICML
finding: Gradient-free library learning by LLM refactoring: write helper functions over batches, test them by execution, retry, edit, prune. Helper functions plus refactored demos then go into the prompt of the program-writing agent.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B: LOGO 45.6 to 57.1 (+11.5), Date 42.8 to 68.9 (+26.1), TextCraft 18.8 to 26.9 (+8.1). GPT-3.5-turbo: Date 88.9 to 90.2, LOGO 15.4 to 18.4, MATH 43.2 to 55.4, TabMWP 87.4 to 89.2. About 200 training examples. Mean of 3 seeds.
limits: Same in-context budget of 10 examples for both arms, so REGAL arm shows fewer primitive demos. Largest gains for weaker open models. Small gains for strong model on Date. Compute of the learning stage not compared with baseline compute.
agent_relevance: Execution-verified helpers help weak models a lot and strong ones a little. Retry and curriculum matter. Our scaffold targets a strong model, so expect the small-gain end.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2024) ReGAL ablations and distribution shift
finding: Every component adds value. The retry loop and the easy-to-hard curriculum matter most. Pruning and editing the library helps under shift.
numbers: Ablation (CodeLlama-13B, dev, LOGO/Date/TextCraft): full 55.0/77.0/34.12; minus retry 48.3/51.9/30.43; minus curriculum 36.3/56.6/28.78; minus prune 52.0/65.5/25.26; minus edit 53.3/69.6/27.35. Shift to unseen TextCraft objects: primitives 7.8, REGAL 11.4, plus pruning on unseen dev 14.9, full re-run 17.2. With 25 demos gain +2.56; about half the data +8.45.
limits: Dev splits, small N.
agent_relevance: Order tasks short to long when building a store, prune on fresh data, and expect wrong-helper-call as the main new failure mode.

source: Wang, Fried, Neubig (2024) TroVE: Inducing Verifiable and Efficient Toolboxes
finding: Training-free toolbox induction with three modes (create, import, skip), periodic trimming, and agreement-based selection. Reports higher accuracy and much smaller toolboxes than an instance-level tool-making baseline.
numbers: 11 datasets (math, table QA, image reasoning). 79-98% smaller toolboxes. Math: 30-120% more correct than primitive baseline across 7 datasets (CodeLlama-7B). Humans verified TroVE solutions 31% faster and 13% more accurately. Instance-level tool baseline often worse than primitives (hundreds or thousands of tools).
limits: Gains later disputed (see c12, c14): reuse is rare and the baseline had less compute. CodeLlama-7B is a weak base model.
agent_relevance: Trimming a library beats growing it without bound: too many low-utility tools confuse the model. Keep any store small and pruned.

source: Wang et al. (2024) LEGO-Prover: Neural Theorem Proving with Growing Libraries
finding: Isabelle prover with a growing skill library: a prover uses retrieved lemmas, an evolver creates and revises lemmas. Reported new best miniF2F pass rates and a skill-library ablation gain.
numbers: miniF2F-valid 48.0 to 57.0% and test 45.5 to 50.0% (ChatGPT, 100 attempts). Ablation at 50 attempts: 47.1% without skill library vs 50.4% with. 22,532 skills generated; 10.8% from prover, 38.2% from evolver solve-request, 51.1% from directional transformation.
limits: Compared to baselines at equal attempt counts, not equal compute. Ablation gap is 3.3 points on one split. Later work finds reuse is almost absent (c12, c13).
agent_relevance: Strong result on paper that fails an independent compute-matched test. Treat self-reported library gains as unproven until reuse is measured.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library Learning Doesn't: The Curious Case of the Single-Use Library
finding: Direct reuse of learned tools is almost nil in both LEGO-Prover and TroVE. Gains look like self-correction and self-consistency instead.
numbers: LEGO-Prover logs: over 20,000 lemmas learned, only 1,233 (6%) appear in prover prompts, exactly 1 lemma reused verbatim once, none twice. Zero-reuse ablation (GPT-4o-mini, 12 problems, 50 attempts, 2 trials) solved only 1 fewer problem. TroVE re-run on MATH: 15 functions learned, 2 reused in 3 correct solutions out of 3,201 test questions.
limits: Subsets and small trials; GPT-4o-mini replaces deprecated GPT-3.5. Indirect reuse (library as examples) not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Biggest warning for us: measure whether stored items are actually used in later solutions before crediting memory. Log reuse counts as a metric in every library test.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2025) LLM Library Learning Fails: A LEGO-Prover Case Study
finding: No direct reuse and no soft reuse (modifying retrieved lemmas) of learned lemmas. LEGO-Prover's advantage over a simple Draft-Sketch-Prove baseline disappears when compute is matched.
numbers: Baseline Draft-Sketch-Prove with 4o-mini 35.9 +/- 0.9% vs 45.5% (50% with human proofs) claimed for LEGO-Prover. Each LEGO-Prover attempt costs about 6x the GPU compute of baseline (14x with o3-mini). Matched for compute, baseline equals or beats LEGO-Prover. Verbatim lemma use 2/43 (GPT-4o 20% split), 4/21, 0/20 (o3-mini), 13/189 (4o-mini full set); name use 9/43, 6/21, 5/20, 47/189. 3 trials, subsets 5-20% of test for costly models.
limits: Subsets of miniF2F test because of cost; one system studied in depth. Baseline could not be beaten at equal GPU spend, not proven that no library can help.
agent_relevance: Any library claim must be tested against the same model given the same token budget for plain retries. Add this equal-budget arm to our bench.

source: Sesterhenn, Berlot-Attwell, Zenkner, Bartelt (2025) A Compute-Matched Re-Evaluation of TroVE on MATH
finding: TroVE's advantage over the primitive baseline comes from using more LLM calls. With compute matched the benefit shrinks to about 1 point and is not significant. Fixing a bug in TroVE's selection step (two-stage voting instead of one-stage) added 3 points to TroVE.
numbers: K=15 samples per task, 5 seeds. MATH overall: original primitive baseline 0.12; compute-matched primitive 0.24. TroVE reproduced 0.22, corrected 0.25. Gain over baseline about 1 point, not significant. TroVE produces 0.74 more distinct candidates per task, which also makes selection harder.
limits: CodeLlama-7B on MATH only. Toolbox benefit might exist in other domains.
agent_relevance: The original baseline got one mode, the method got three. Always count calls per arm. Diverse samples can hurt selection unless the check is strong.

source: Sesterhenn et al. (2025) TroVE per-mode analysis
finding: Create, import and skip modes each solve overlapping problem sets; mode diversity does not by itself explain the gain. Authors conclude the benefit is best explained by higher compute budget and sampling, not the toolbox.
numbers: Compute-matched MATH 0.24 for primitive vs about 0.25 for corrected TroVE; per category differences mostly within one standard deviation (5 seeds).
limits: Single benchmark, single model family, workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: more samples from one model are not independent evidence, and gains attributed to a mechanism may be sampling.

source: Zenkner et al. (2024) AbstractBeam: Enhancing Bottom-Up Program Synthesis Using Library Learning
finding: Adds Stitch-style library learning and wake-sleep to LambdaBeam. Abstractions cut search depth, so fewer candidates and less time are needed, but only on tasks that actually use abstractions.
numbers: Handwritten test tasks (2-fold, 5 runs): fold 1 LambdaBeam 50.2 +/- 2.0% vs AbstractBeam 53.6 +/- 2.3% (p<0.05); fold 2 36.0 +/- 2.5% vs 39.6 +/- 1.5% (p<0.05). Mean solve time on commonly solved tasks 2.57 s vs 4.57 s. Synthetic out-of-domain tasks: 52.6 vs 53.8 (fold 1), 52.4 vs 51.2 (fold 2), no difference.
limits: Gains of 3.4 and 3.6 points; trained 10 iterations with reduced compute; abstractions from handwritten tasks did not transfer to the synthetic distribution; unused abstractions bloat the DSL and cancel the gain.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: library gains appear only where later tasks share structure with the tasks that built the library. Check task similarity before reusing.

source: Alford et al. (2021) Neural-guided, Bidirectional Program Search for Abstraction and Reasoning
finding: Early use of DreamCoder compression on ARC symmetry tasks. Compression produces general helpers such as flip horizontally and stack horizontally, and later tasks become solvable that enumeration could not reach.
numbers: 36 ARC symmetry tasks, five grid primitives, five iterations: 16 solved initially, 17 after iteration 1, 19 after iteration 2, 22 after final iteration. Warm-up: six synthetic tasks compressed into three directional abstractions.
limits: Very small, hand-picked subset of 36 tasks with a hand-chosen five-primitive DSL. No held-out test of the learned library reported.
agent_relevance: First direct ARC case for library learning; shows value is tied to a fixed small DSL. Matches our ARC portfolio caution.

source: Pang (2025) ARC-AGI-2 SoTA: Efficient Evolutionary Program Synthesis (DreamCoder-inspired Python library)
finding: LLM-driven program synthesis with a library that starts empty. For each task the prompt includes the best program(s) already in the library; the best new program is added back. Prompt also shows failed examples and the expected versus actual output difference, which the author says helps a lot.
numbers: Final submission with Grok-4: 77.1% on ARC-AGI-1 semi-private, 26.0% on ARC-AGI-2 semi-private. About 10 LLM calls per task (5 programs x 2 rounds), estimated $2.56 per task on ARC-AGI-1. Comparison approaches about $29 and $400 per task. Score-weighted softmax sampling of library programs beat greedy. Dev runs on 40 ARC-AGI-1 training tasks.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed. No ablation of the library itself reported, so the gain from the library versus plain repeated sampling with feedback is unknown. Library holds whole task programs, not compressed functions.
agent_relevance: Cheap, simple form of library use (reuse best prior program as an example) at a strong cost point. Real revision signal (output diff) is the part the author credits, in line with G2.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent induces reusable workflows (routines with abstracted example values) from past successful trajectories and gives them to the agent as memory. Works offline or online.
numbers: WebArena (gpt-4-0613, temperature 0): total success 35.5% vs BrowserGym 23.5% baseline (+12.0 points, 51.1% relative). About 2.0 fewer steps per task than BrowserGym. Beats human-written workflows (SteP, 32.0) by 7.6% relative. Mind2Web relative gain 24.6%. Online AWM surpasses baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 points as train-test gap widens.
limits: Workflows are text, induced by the same LLM; no direct reuse count in main table. Web navigation with repeated site templates, which favours routine reuse.
agent_relevance: Procedural memory from the agent's own successful runs helps when tasks recur. Success must be verified before storing.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks (ASI)
finding: Skills stored as executable programs and verified by re-running them before being added. Beats both a static agent and a text-workflow memory (AWM) on WebArena with fewer steps.
numbers: claude-3.5-sonnet. WebArena success: vanilla 32.7%, AWM 36.3%, ASI 40.4% (+7.7 points, 23.5% relative; +4.1 vs AWM, 11.3% relative). Steps 5.6 vs 5.9 vs 5.0. Verification ablation (shopping): unverified text 32.6, verified program 36.4, verified text 39.0, verified program added as actions 40.1. Programs pass verification on only 15.6% of turns; at least one skill reused in 42.5% of cases; skills induced from 7.6% of tasks. Cross-website: ASI success edge over AWM not significant (p=0.1673), step reduction is (p=0.0378).
limits: Text of the paper reports a 4.2-point verification gain but the table gives 3.8. Web tasks with repeated structure; one backbone model. Read via an HTML fetch summary, not a full local PDF.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that verified, executable stored skills beat prose memories, and that reuse can be counted (42.5%). Verification gate matches G3.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs
finding: Skill library of verified JavaScript functions, indexed by description embeddings, plus automatic curriculum and self-verification, in Minecraft with GPT-4.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines. Tech tree speedups: wooden 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x; only Voyager reached diamond (1 of 3 trials, 102 iterations). Without skill library: wooden 7+/-2, stone 9+/-4, iron 29+/-11 iterations vs Voyager 6+/-2, 11+/-2, 21+/-7; no diamond. Zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks: 3/3 trials at 18-30 iterations; baselines failed within 50. Ablations: random curriculum -93% items, no self-verification -73%, GPT-3.5 for code gives 5.7x fewer items.
limits: 3 trials per method. Skill-library ablation shows a gain mainly in later stages (iron and diamond), smaller than the curriculum and verification ablations. No reuse counts reported. Read through a fetch summary of the first 100k characters.
agent_relevance: The curriculum and verification mattered more than the library itself, in line with the ReGAL curriculum result. Skills reused across tasks carried over to new worlds.

source: Andrews (2024) Capturing Sparks of Abstraction for the ARC Challenge
finding: Gives an LLM (Gemini-Flash-002) complete DSL solutions to ARC tasks and asks it to explain them at several abstraction levels: commented code, refactored reusable chunks, solution steps, tactics. Builds an LLM-legible rename of Hodel's arc-dsl (85 functions renamed).
numbers: No solve-rate numbers reported; dataset covers the 400 ARC training-task solutions with multilevel explanations. Says LLMs struggle to understand many tasks from grids alone.
limits: Resource and method paper; no accuracy on held-out tasks, no ablation. Only scanned for method and numbers.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as LILO: names must be readable to the model. Source of readable abstraction labels for ARC, but untested for transfer.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: how much of the gain is library versus model, search or compute
finding: Across the LLM-era studies the pattern is consistent. Verified, readable, small libraries help weak models and structure-heavy domains. Claimed gains for strong models often shrink or vanish once compute and sampling are matched, and reuse counts are rarely reported.
numbers: LILO: library over bare LLM +0.94 (REGEX) to +16.82 (LOGO). ReGAL: +11.5 to +26.1 for CodeLlama-13B but +1.3 to +3.0 for GPT-3.5 on LOGO, Date, TabMWP-class sets. TroVE compute-matched: +1. LEGO-Prover compute-matched: 0 or negative. ASI vs vanilla: +7.7 (verified programs).
limits: Own summary of numbers opened above; settings and metrics differ across studies.
agent_relevance: Design implication: build the library only for a repeated task class, gate entries by execution, show reuse rates, and bench against an equal-token resample arm.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO online results against the strongest no-library control
finding: Enumerative search kept inside the loop helps where the target needs code structures the LLM does not propose from language. Library plus LLM beats LLM with search alone mostly on LOGO.
numbers: LLM Solver (+ Search) best: 76.60 / 96.44 / 37.84 (REGEX/CLEVR/LOGO). LILO 77.07 / 96.76 / 48.95. So the library adds about 0.5, 0.3 and 11 points over that stronger baseline.
limits: LLM Solver (+Search) has no library but includes enumeration, so it is the fairest control. Numbers are means over runs on 3 domains.
agent_relevance: The fairest control shows the library margin is small outside hard-structure domains. Relevant when judging our own before/after tests.

source: Berlot-Attwell et al. (2024) TroVE ablation without IMPORT mode
finding: With the import mode removed, the ablated TroVE matched or beat the full method on three of four MATH splits, so the library read path was not needed. Libraries formed only for counting, number and prealgebra.
numbers: TroVE reproduced (5 trials): count 0.236, geometry 0.058, intermediate 0.120, number 0.258. No-reuse ablation: 0.250, 0.050, 0.134, 0.290. No functions learned for algebra, geometry, intermediate algebra, precalculus. Reused functions were is_perfect_square and is_prime.
limits: Welch t-test on 5 trials, Bonferroni-corrected; CodeLlama-7B; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: On math, a model already knows the helpers a library could learn. Libraries matter where the domain vocabulary is not in the weights.

source: Wang et al. (2024) LEGO-Prover authors' own skill use analysis
finding: Authors' case study notes many retrieved skills cannot be reused directly but serve as reference for writing new, similar lemmas (soft reuse).
numbers: Among solved valid problems: 24% used retrieved skills; of these 51% reused them directly and 49% built new lemmas. Of direct uses, 71% came from do-requests; scaling complexity 12%; parameterization 6%.
limits: Soft reuse later contradicted: Berlot-Attwell (2025) find soft-reuse curves reach zero while 30-40% of tasks still show some similarity (c13).
agent_relevance: Soft reuse is hard to separate from the model solving a similar problem unaided. Use a no-library control.

source: Ellis et al. (2020/2023) DreamCoder: recognition model bootstraps libraries; dreams
finding: Dreaming (training on imagined tasks built from the current library) lets the recognition model learn when to call new routines. Libraries get deeper when a recognition model is present; dreams grow more complex with training.
numbers: Library depth correlated with tasks solved r=0.79; library size correlation weaker. Physics run starting from 1959-Lisp-style recursion relearns fold, unfold and origami programming after roughly five days on 64 CPUs.
limits: The neural recognition model needs many generated tasks; not directly portable to prompt-only agents.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold has no trained recognizer. A retrieval step over stored helper descriptions is the nearest substitute, and the AWM and ASI results show it can work.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2024) ReGAL error analysis and limitations
finding: Benefits come from both reuse and simplified reasoning. Errors with the library: wrong connector code, undefined or similar-but-wrong function, false-negative verifier. Not every domain has reusable abstractions.
numbers: LOGO, CodeLlama-13B: 25 cases where ReGAL was right and baseline wrong (16 baseline reasoning errors, 9 shape errors). 13 cases the other way: 7 connector code, 4 wrong or undefined function, 2 verifier false negatives.
limits: Manual categorization on one domain and model.
agent_relevance: Expected failure modes for a stored-helper agent: calling the wrong helper and checker mistakes. Add a check that the helper's contract matches the call.

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Stitch early stopping; Grand et al. (2024) deep refactoring each iteration
finding: Stitch can be stopped early with graceful loss, so compression can run as an anytime step inside a loop. LILO re-derives the whole library from the base language every iteration, which discards early poor abstractions.
numbers: Stitch finds abstractions in tens of milliseconds across five domains; LILO reports typical Stitch runs of seconds on one CPU per iteration.
limits: Stitch operates on lambda calculus syntax trees; applying it to free-form Python or prose requires conversion.
agent_relevance: Rebuilding the library from the solved set each round is cheap and avoids lock-in on early picks. Matches a no-fixed-library design.

source: Zenkner et al. (2024) AbstractBeam boundary condition on DSL bloat
finding: Adding abstractions widens the search but shortens depth. Gain holds only if abstractions are used; unused abstractions cancel the benefit.
numbers: Significant gains only at program lengths whose solutions contain abstractions (62% of length-7 programs contain them); gains vanish where few do; no difference on the synthetic set (52.6 vs 53.8).
quote: This highlights the care that must be taken when designing the initial and altering the current DSL.
limits: Reduced compute versus original LambdaBeam, one domain (integer lists).
agent_relevance: Prune by measured use, not by compression gain alone.
